meta.title: There's no point at which turning your brain off will work
meta.author: binjip978

comments.author: roryokane
comments.text:
“No point” seems like an exaggeration born of wishful thinking. If LLMs become good enough to perform all the functions of an employee, there will still be a transitionary period in which employees have realized that the LLM is good enough but employers have not. Depending on the agility of the company, it could be a week or a year. A perfectly efficient company would not have such a period, but companies are not perfectly efficient.

An employee successfully delegating 100% of their job to an LLM would be an example of arbitrage. The presence of arbitrage in other existing markets suggests that we don’t know how to eliminate arbitrage in the job market, either.

Also, even if LLMs become good enough to do only 90% of the work, a selfish employee who doesn’t plan to stay at their current company might find it worthwhile to turn their brain off. The company will eventually notice the employee’s decreased performance and fire them, but the employee would get some extra paychecks for no effort. If they already have another job lined up or they are near retirement, they might not be worried about how that would affect their reputation.

comments.author: spillybones
comments.text:
there will still be a transitionary period in which employees have realized that the LLM is good enough but employers have not


We are currently witnessing employers laying off employees based on the false belief that LLMs can do the employees' jobs. Employers are so ready to believe that LLMs are good enough that they're jumping the gun. I don't think there's going to be a point where bosses could stop paying employees but aren't ready to believe it.

comments.author: singpolyma
comments.text: Hasn't this basically always been an excuse used to justify a layoff they wanted to do anyway? All the ones I read about were basically corrections after pandemic over hiring with a veneer of "because AI" in the press release.

comments.author: alandekok
comments.text:
We are currently witnessing employers laying off employees based on the false belief that LLMs can do the employees' jobs.


I've seen employers lay off 20% of the workforce, and then be surprised when they see AI bills that are higher than the salaries of the people that they laid off.

At the same time, it's extremely difficult to be a junior developer now.  If it takes a junior developer a week to write a tool / feature, but a senior developer can do the same thing in an hour with AI, where's the room for a junior developer?

Employers aren't in the business of running charities.  While it might seem sociopathic, there are sound reasons for laying off people when 90% or more what they do can be replaced with AI, and a few hours work by a senior developer.

The question then is how do companies get new senior developers, if the juniors are laid off?  There's no easy answer to that.

comments.author: orib
comments.text:
The question then is how do companies get new senior developers, if the juniors are laid off? There's no easy answer to that.


The bet being placed is that the seniors will be redundant before this becomes a problem.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: The bet being placed by the actual people making this decision, is that the current CEOs will be in a different industry faster than this problem becomes visible enough. Whether seniors will be redundant is the company's problems for after the stock options vest.

comments.author: orib
comments.text:
Currently the people pushing hard for LLM use are the corporations, because they want to remove the employees. They're going to be watching real close for any sign that the employees are now redundant.

There'll be a "just in case" window when the employer isn't sure that just removing the human will work out, but I doubt it'll be a large one.

comments.text: Only if we get a move on before policing is automated.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: Automated and scaled up, without cutting corners. They want to believe it is about policing riots. But at that level of collapse it will be about policing people with nothing to lose taking long stretches of power grid that were live just before.

comments.author: mordae
comments.text: As usual, future comes non-evenly. Some places will see it earlier, others will watch and take notes. Both authoritarians and democrats.

comments.author: singpolyma
comments.text:
If we hold all else equal it is very very bad for people. However an economy that works without people is also a description of the post scarcity dream. The problem is that if we keep making "jobs" the way anyone gets the benefit of the economy and no one has one we end up with a disaster rather than liberation.

We can't keep pushing tech progress alone and hoping society figures out the rest. We need to work on society first before the tech progress can be beneficial for humanity.

comments.author: orib
comments.text: I think I'd last a year or two in that kind of world before killing myself.

comments.author: singpolyma
comments.text: What kind of a world? One where you don't constantly fear going hungry? Or maybe I've described what I'm talking about poorly and there is some misunderstanding here.

comments.text:
One where you don't constantly fear going hungry?

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
But would it be all problems or all scale-friendly problems?

Getting a 3D printer and access to a model repository does not solve all your problems solvable by a small piece of plastic, only those someone has already formulated.

A benevolent automated takeover of supplying the obvious necessities and requested luxuries would need to work under a similar constraint not to become social media algorithmic feed, yet again. The real issue is, of course, how many organisations to outlaw to not have social media algorithmic feed (but physical) as the explicit target outcome.

comments.author: orib
comments.text:
You're describing a universe where a sufficiently capable AI decides of its own volition to fuck off, except in the worst circumstances. That's not what we're building.

We're laser focused on having the algorithmic social media feed, but more addictive.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
They are also laser focused on buying more RAM than they can buy power supplies for. We should get better at using the logic of guardrails-adding panics to ensure more refusals, there I agree. Although it is not about just LLMs, it is about giga-corporate-friendly culture in general. And I agree that the boring-world outcome is not the primary outlook, DotCom 2.0 and LLM Fukushima are both relatively positive but more likely.

Addictivity-wise, overfitting machines are pushed to overfit for addictiveness to those who do not share your aversion to not having problems to solve. Ideally, sycophancy would shift the feed to emotional manipulation ascribed to cute animals. The problems remaining for humans to usefully handle might be (in the optimistic scenario) niche and less pressing, but well, you would be looking to improve comfort of your subculture, and this would probably be one of the subcultures that bread-and-circuses machine doesn't understand (possibly for lack of trying).

But in any case I was responding to your comment about the arguably-utopian outcome being horrible, so I am not meaningfully commenting on the question «what parts of critical infrastructure are most vulnerable to scavenging in the remote places if the economy providing anything useful to actual people just crashes». Which, unfortunately, might end up a more relevant question.

comments.author: orib
comments.text: Comment removed by its author

comments.author: emk
comments.text:
Yup. If the robots are ever cheaper and more efficient than human labor, then the robots can just build the private jets and mansions for the billionaires directly, no human workers required. And if the humans complain about being hungry, then arm the robots.

The assumption that you need humans to run an economy is based on the idea that humans are the most intelligent, flexible and cost-effective workers available. If the humans are the only good workforce available, then it's important to keep the humans happy and productive. But if humans are ever outcompeted economically by sufficiently advanced AI and robots, then the billionaires don't necessarily need all 8 billion of us.

Of course, there's also the question of whether the billionaires could control the robots any better than OpenAI has been controlling its swarms of agents.

comments.author: toastal
comments.text: This is why I am skeptical of something like UBI taking off since it presupposes that those in power think the masses deserve not just to live but basic dignity in doing so. Under the current economic climate, this does not align with the goals of creating more capital, more wealth for those in power—which has been basically the only metric measured & cared about for the last several decades.
